summary_html: Agency chooses **Differential Response (DR)**/**Alternative Response**: engage **services without court petition** when safety permits. FFPSA and IV-B/IV-E prevention funding support voluntary, front-end help to avert removals.
authority_html:
- **Family First Prevention Services Act (FFPSA)** — prevention services framework under IV-E  
- **SSA Title IV-B & IV-E (42 U.S.C. §§ 620–629m; 670–679c)** — service funding & case-plan requirements  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — assesses safety/permanency outcomes in DR systems

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
key_cases.holding: Reversing a one-page order dismissing an abuse and neglect petition, the Court held that a circuit court that sees reasonable cause to believe additional abuse or neglect exists may compel DHHR to investigate and amend the petition, and must enter findings of fact and conclusions of law on the allegations.
key_cases.relevance: An agency preference for informal resolution cannot end a case without judicial findings.
key_cases.quote: the circuit court has the inherent authority to compel the Department to amend its petition to encompass the evidence or allegations

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
key_cases.holding: The Court held that DHHR kept its statutory responsibility for filing the case plan even after a private agency was made case manager, that foster parents may participate in abuse and neglect proceedings in a limited way, and that a child has a right to continued contact with those with whom he has formed a close bond when that serves his best interests.
key_cases.relevance: Choosing a service route outside court compulsion does not shift the agency's statutory planning duties onto a contracted provider.
key_cases.quote: we believe that DHHR nonetheless retained its statutory responsibility with regard to the filing of a case plan with the court under West Virginia Code § 49-6-5

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
key_cases.holding: Affirming denial of post-adjudicatory and dispositional improvement periods and the termination of parental rights, the Court held that an improvement period is a carefully limited, discretionary opportunity that must be denied where granting it would jeopardize the child's best interests.
key_cases.relevance: It marks the limits of the service-first path once the child's safety interest is engaged.
key_cases.quote: Where an improvement period would jeopardize the best interests of the child, for instance, an improvement period will not be granted

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
key_cases.holding: Remanding for a proper adjudicatory hearing, the Court held that a circuit court may not reach any dispositional alternative until it has held a hearing and determined whether the child is abused or neglected, and that a voluntary arrangement among the parties cannot bypass that threshold question.
key_cases.relevance: A voluntary dispositional plan is permitted only with court approval and cannot be used by the parties or the agency to circumvent the threshold abuse-or-neglect question.
key_cases.quote: have determined "whether such child is abused or neglected." Such a finding is the prerequisite to any further proceedings in the case.
